newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM hails first rise in GDP under reforms.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM hails first rise in GDP under reforms.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday that Russia's gross domestic product (GDP), the broadest measure of economic health, had started rising for the first first time since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

"This has happened for the first time in five years of reforms," Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin as saying in his surprise announcement, which confounded experts' predictions and seemed improbable in the light of figures in recent months.

President Boris Yeltsin responded to Chernomyrdin's rosy assessment by telling the government to tackle its toughest task -- ending wage arrears to the army within two months and to other public sector workers within three months.

Yeltsin also acted decisively in the political sphere by sacking justice minister Valentin Kovalyov, who was allegedly filmed in a gangland sauna with naked women. He replaced him with his old ally, former security service chief Sergei Stepashin.

Kovalyov's dismissal removed the last communist from the government. Yeltsin had sacked the only other communist, Aman Tuleyev, as minister for Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) affairs on Tuesday.
Yeltsin's no-nonsense actions encapsulated the strength and resolve of the 66-year-old Kremlin leader at the end of the first year of his four-year second term as president.

Yeltsin, who beat a communist candidate to win re-election on July 3 last year, has taken a firm grip on power since recovering from the heart trouble which forced him out of his Kremlin office until February and put his leadership in question.
Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin met in the Kremlin to discuss the economy for the second successive day.
"On the whole, we have finished the half-year with positive results," Interfax quoted Chernomyrdin as saying.

Chernomyrdin, a loyal but uninspiring premier since 1992, later announced the rise in GDP -- the total value of goods and services produced in the first half of this year -- at a science awards ceremony. He gave no basis for his calculation.

Official statistics showed a fall in GDP for the first five months. Many Russian officials have predicted flat output in 1997 and forecast no growth until next year, although many feel official figures underplay thriving service sector businesses.
A rise in GDP would be a big boost for the reformist team Yeltsin created under a cabinet reshuffle in February and March.
But Yeltsin made clear the government must not rest on its laurels. He said increasing tax collection, which is below target, was vital to provide money for the state budget.
He also set the government a tough task by telling it to pay off the wage arrears in the armed forces and the public sector.

"The president has set two new top priorities: to pay state debt to the armed forces personnel within two months and to cover state debts to teachers, doctors and other workers of the budget sphere," the Kremlin press service said in a statement.
Wage arrears to the military amount to five trillion roubles ($860 million), and the state's total debt to the army is calculated at tens of trillions of roubles.
The government said last week it had met another of Yeltsin's demands by paying off a huge backlog of pensions.

But the government still faces many problems. Interfax said dozens of angry nuclear power station workers were preparing for a 350-km (220-mile) protest march from their workplace to Moscow to demand four month of unpaid wages.
The government says its efforts are hindered by the communist-led State Duma, the lower house of parliament, which has opposed efforts to cut budget spending and social benefits.

The Duma is on holiday until September 1 and deputies have resisted efforts to break their holiday to pass urgently needed reform legislation. Yeltsin is likely to raise the issue when he meets communist Duma speaker Gennady Seleznyov on Friday.
